mcp-context-engineering-q22.testing: that a prompt is a deployed artefact: versioned, gated by an eval, rolled out gradually, and attributable on every response.
mcp-context-engineering-q22.trap: treating the prompt as config that anyone edits in a console, and losing attribution.
mcp-context-engineering-q22.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask who edits prompts, how often, and what depends on the output: a parser, a tool schema, a downstream service."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The constraint is that a prompt is code with no compiler. One edited string can drop quality for a week before anyone notices, unless something measures it."
3 · Baseline design "So prompts are deployable artefacts. They live in version control, every edit creates an immutable version, and every trace records which version served it. A change runs through an eval gate in CI: a golden set with assertions and a calibrated judge. A regression fails the merge, not the users."
4 · Deep-dive "Rollout is like code: a canary on a small share, comparing task success and complaint signals, then a ramp, with rollback by moving a pointer. And I version the coupled unit. The prompt, the tool definitions and the model version move together, because a prompt is tuned to one model."
5 · Failure modes "It fails when someone edits in a console with no history, when the model changes underneath an untouched prompt, or when a prompt change alters the output shape the parser expects."
6 · Evolve "The aim isn't to restrict who edits. It's to make the safe path the easy one, so a product manager can change wording because the gate catches the damage."
Close "Every response should point to an exact prompt version, or evaluation is guesswork."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Three answers shape the process."

Question Sets
Who edits: engineers, product, domain experts? whether authoring needs a UI and a proposer role
How often? whether prompt release must be independent of code deploys
What parses or depends on the output? which changes must ship with code

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"The gate has to be able to see the size of change it's meant to catch."

golden set of 200 cases at about 80% accuracy:
SE = √(0.8 × 0.2 / 200) = 0.028 → about ±5.5 points at 95%
a 15-point drop is far outside that → the gate catches it
a 3-point drop is inside it → needs more cases, or a paired comparison

Cost of the gate: one eval run per prompt change, off the user path, so no added user latency.

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"Four things a prompt gets that copy text doesn't."

Release:edit in the repopull requesteval gate in CIimmutable version publishedcanaryrampmove the pointer back
Practice Detail
Version control prompts in git or a registry; every edit is a new immutable version
Attribution the prompt version and model version on every trace
Template and variables separated a data change isn't a logic change
Eval gate assertions first, a calibrated judge for the rest, a threshold above run-to-run noise

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
"Offline says it may ship; the canary says it's safe with real traffic."

Stage Traffic Watch
Offline gate the golden set every gate metric
Canary a small share, by user or session task success, escalations, thumbs-down, cost
Ramp the rest the same
Rollback — move the label back; takes one cache lifetime
Moves together Why
Prompt + model version a prompt is tuned to one model
Prompt + tool definitions the prompt refers to tools by name and behaviour
Prompt + parser an output-shape change must ship with the code that reads it

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"Three incidents this process exists to prevent."

Failure Control
A string edited in a console; quality falls for a week no production edit path outside the release process
The model alias changed under an untouched prompt pin model versions; re-run the gate when the model moves
A wording change altered the output fields contract changes ship with code: parser accepts both, then switch
"Quality dropped on Tuesday", cause unknown version on every trace → "v17 dropped the parse rate"
The gate is flaky and gets disabled thresholds from measured variance; deterministic assertions as hard gates

stages.name: Evolve
stages.claim: make the safe path the easy path
stages.html:
"Governance that people don't route around."

Role Can do
Anyone with domain knowledge propose a version; see its eval result
Reviewer or owner promote a version that passed
CI publish versions; attach the eval run

Evaluation hook: the golden set, grown from production failures. Fix layer: release process. The registry mechanics are in decouple-prompt-releases and the wider process in eval-driven-prompt-development.

followUps.question: "It's one sentence; just change it in the admin panel."
followUps.html:
One sentence can move unrelated cases, and nothing will tell you.

Console edit Released version
No history a diff
No test an eval run attached
No rollback target the previous version

followUps.question: 🧪 Quality fell on Tuesday. The trace shows prompt v17 from Monday and a model snapshot that changed Tuesday. Which one?
followUps.html:
The model, on that evidence, and that's only knowable because both are on the trace.

Mon: prompt v16 → v17, quality steady
Tue: model snapshot changed, quality falls        ← the change that coincides

Then confirm by running the golden set on both snapshots with v17.

followUps.question: Who can edit prompts?
followUps.html:
Many people can propose; few can promote; nobody skips the gate.

  • Authoring is open.
  • Promotion is privileged and logged.

followUps.question: How do you A/B test a contested change?
followUps.html:
Split by user or session, and measure behaviour.

Rule Why
Randomise by user, not request one person shouldn't see both prompts
Cluster the statistics on that unit requests from one user aren't independent

followUps.question: The provider deprecates the model in two months. What happens to the prompts?
followUps.html:
Every prompt is re-gated against the new model, as a dated migration.

Plan:run all golden sets on the new model with prompts frozenlist regressionstune, often by deleting scaffoldscanaryswitch

dontSay: "Prompts are just config." — they define behaviour.
"We edit them in the console." — with what history and what test?
"Quality dropped and we don't know why." — that's missing attribution.
"Only engineers may touch prompts." — the gate, not the gatekeeper, is the control.

mcp-context-engineering-q23.testing: that retention is paid on every step and retrieval once, and that you decide per item by size, stability and how often it's needed.
mcp-context-engineering-q23.trap: keeping every retrieved document in context "in case it's needed again".
mcp-context-engineering-q23.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Frame the axis "Keeping something in context costs tokens on every step for the rest of the run. Retrieving it again costs latency once, when it's needed. So it's a per-item decision."
2 · Where keeping wins "I keep what's small, stable and needed on every step: the goal, the constraints, a schema, the decisions made so far."
3 · Where re-retrieving wins "I retrieve again what's large, changeable, or needed only occasionally: documents, records, tool results. In a long run this nearly always wins, because retained documents are what causes context rot."
4 · The deciding question "For each item I ask three things. How big is it? Can it change during the run? And on what share of the remaining steps will it actually be used?"
5 · What I'd pick "My default is the middle ground. I keep a compact pointer or a one-line summary in context, with an id, and fetch the full body on demand. That way the model knows the thing exists and how to get it."
Close "Keep pointers, fetch bodies."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: paid every step, or paid once
stages.html:
"Two different bills."

Keep in context Retrieve again
Cost tokens on every remaining step a lookup and its latency, when needed
Freshness a snapshot from when it was read current
Risk rot and distraction a miss, if retrieval fails
Pick when small, stable, always needed large, changeable, occasional

stages.name: Where keeping wins
stages.html:
"Four things that earn a permanent place."

Keep Why
The goal and success criteria every step depends on them
Constraints discovered so far forgetting one is a wrong action
A schema or a short policy needed for every call, rarely changes
Decisions and ids the run's working state

These also sit well in the cached prefix or a pinned block, so their per-step cost is low.

stages.name: Where re-retrieving wins
stages.html:
"The arithmetic favours retrieval quickly."

a 4,000-token document, 30 steps remaining                       (illustrative)
keep it:        4,000 × 30 = 120,000 token-steps
re-retrieve it: needed on 3 of those steps → 4,000 × 3 = 12,000, plus 3 lookups
keep a pointer: 200 × 30 = 6,000, plus a fetch when needed
Re-retrieve Why
Documents and long records large; used on a few steps
Tool results can be fetched again; may have changed
Anything that can go stale a fresh read beats a snapshot

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.html:
"Three properties per item."

Size Changes during the run? Used on most steps? Decision
Small no yes keep
Small yes yes keep, and refresh on change
Large no yes keep a summary; fetch detail
Large either no re-retrieve
Any yes, and correctness depends on it — re-retrieve before acting

stages.name: What I'd pick
stages.claim: pointers in context, bodies on demand
stages.html:
"The model should know what exists and how to get it."

Pattern:retrieveusereplace the body with [doc kb-17: refund policy, 2 lines]later, fetch kb-17 again if needed
Element of a pointer Purpose
A stable id the fetch key
A one-line summary enough to decide whether to fetch
A date or version staleness is visible
Compare on long-run cases Keep everything Pointers + fetch
Task success at step 30 measure measure
Tokens per run measure measure
Fetches per run — measure

Fix layer: context assembly and retrieval. The eviction side is in step-40-what-to-throw-away.

followUps.question: "Keep the documents; re-retrieving is slow."
followUps.html:
Retaining is slower in total: every later step processes them again.

Keep Fetch on demand
Latency added to every step latency added to a few steps
Old documents distract later steps only current ones are present

followUps.question: 🧪 A 6,000-token record is needed on 10 of 20 remaining steps. Keep or fetch?
followUps.html:
Fetching still halves the tokens; then latency decides.

keep:  6,000 × 20 = 120,000 token-steps
fetch: 6,000 × 10 =  60,000 token-steps + 10 lookups

At that frequency I'd keep a structured extract of the fields actually used, which is smaller than either.

followUps.question: What if the data changes mid-run?
followUps.html:
Then a retained copy is a liability.

  • Before any action that depends on it, read it again.
  • A balance or stock level from ten steps ago isn't safe to act on.

followUps.question: Doesn't dropping documents hurt prompt caching?
followUps.html:
Only if it rewrites the prefix; bodies belong after it.

Layout:stable prefix (cached)pointers and summarythis step's fetched bodiescurrent turn

followUps.question: How do you make sure the model actually re-fetches?
followUps.html:
Give it a fetch tool, a visible pointer, and measure.

Mechanism Check
fetch(id) tool, with pointers listing ids fetch rate when the content was needed
Eval cases that need a dropped document does the agent go and get it?

dontSay: "We keep everything, to be safe." — that's what makes long runs worse.
"We retrieve everything fresh every step." — the goal and constraints shouldn't depend on a lookup.
"The model remembers what it read." — only what's still in the window.
"It depends." — on size, stability and frequency; say which.

mcp-context-engineering-q24.testing: tiers with budgets and eviction, a cache-friendly order, tenant scoping, version tagging, and measurement that makes rot visible.
mcp-context-engineering-q24.trap: a memory design with no eviction, no budget and no measurement.
mcp-context-engineering-q24.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · Clarify "I'd ask how long sessions run, whether the assistant must remember across sessions, how many tenants there are, and which tools and documents it draws on."
2 · Constraints and numbers "The numbers are a window budget well under the limit, a latency target per step, and a cost per session. Every token I keep is paid for on every step."
3 · Baseline design "I'd build three tiers. Working context is this turn: the current question, fetched documents, the latest tool results. Session state is a compacted running summary with the goal, decisions and open items. Long-term memory is an external store, read selectively. A context assembler builds the window from those tiers on every step."
4 · Deep-dive "The assembler is the component that matters. It enforces a budget per tier with hard caps, compacts on a token threshold, orders the window with the stable prefix first for the cache, and pins the goal near the end. It's ordinary code with tests."
5 · Failure modes "It fails through growth with no eviction, a leak across tenants, a summary that loses a constraint, and a cache that never hits because history is rewritten every turn."
6 · Evolve "Everything is tenant-scoped, and prompt, tool and model versions are on every trace. I measure tokens per section per step against quality, so rot shows up on a dashboard before a user reports it."
Close "Three tiers, an assembler with budgets, and composition measured against quality."

stages.name: Clarify
stages.html:
"Four questions size the layer."

Question Sets
How long does a session run, in turns and hours? compaction policy
Must it remember across sessions? whether a long-term store exists
How many tenants and users? isolation keys everywhere
Which tools and document sources? the fixed floor and retrieval budget

Earning it: a short, single-session assistant needs the working tier and a small history cap, and nothing else.

stages.name: Constraints and numbers
stages.html:
"Budgets per tier, set before any content."

window budget per step (illustrative, 128k model)
output reserve            8,000
stable prefix (tools + system, cached)   9,000
long-term memory read     1,000      ← top 3–5 items
session summary           4,000      ← compacted
recent turns verbatim     6,000
working: fetched docs + tool results    20,000
total                    48,000      → 38% of the window; the rest is headroom

latency per step: retrieval + memory read under 300 ms before the model call
cost per session: steps × tokens per step, with the prefix read from cache

stages.name: Baseline design
stages.html:
"State lives outside the window; the assembler decides what enters it."

Tier Holds Lifetime Eviction
Working current question, fetched bodies, latest tool results one turn replaced each turn; bodies become pointers
Session structured summary, goal, decisions, open items, recent turns one session compaction at a token threshold
Long-term facts and past cases, keyed by owner across sessions expiry, reconciliation, deletion on request

stages.name: Deep-dive
stages.html:
"One function decides the window, and it has tests."

Assemble:stable prefixmemory read (top few)session summaryrecent turnsthis turn's documentspinned goal + current questioncount per sectionapply that section's eviction rule
Rule Reason
Stable prefix first, never mutated prompt-cache hits
History append-only between compactions the cached span keeps growing
Goal and constraints pinned near the end used most reliably there
A hard cap per section no silent truncation
Bodies replaced by pointers after use retention is what causes rot
Unit tests on assembly "given this state, the goal is present and total ≤ budget"

stages.name: Failure modes
stages.html:
"What breaks, and the control for each."

Failure Control
The window grows until something is cut caps and eviction per tier
Another tenant's memory or cached answer appears tenant in every key; filters inside the store
The summary lost a constraint a structured summary with fields for constraints and ids; a compaction log
The cache never hits compact in bulk, not every turn; no per-request values in the prefix
A stale memory overrides a fresh fact provenance and dates on memories; newest wins
Quality drops and nobody can say why versions and section sizes on every trace

stages.name: Evolve
stages.html:
"Rot should be visible on a chart before it's a complaint."

Signal, per step Use
Tokens per section which tier is growing
Sampled quality score, by turn number where it starts to fall
Cache-read share is the prefix stable
Compaction events and memory reads used are the policies doing their job

Evaluation hook: long-session and multi-session eval cases (a constraint from turn 2 at turn 40; a fact from session 1 in session 3; no cross-tenant leak). The caps are tuned to one model and re-measured on a change.

Fix layer: context assembly, memory and state management in the harness. The pieces are detailed in the budget, compaction, memory, caching and tenancy answers of this file.

followUps.question: "With a large window we can skip the tiers and keep the whole conversation."
followUps.html:
That's the design with no eviction, no budget and no measurement.

Whole conversation in the window Tiers
Cost and latency grow every turn bounded per step
Stale content accumulates removed by policy
Nothing survives the session long-term memory does

followUps.question: 🧪 In the budget, tool results come back at 35,000 tokens against a 20,000 cap. What happens?
followUps.html:
The assembler applies the working tier's rule; nothing else is squeezed.

working cap 20,000, incoming 35,000
→ truncate each result to its key fields + "more available (cursor)"
→ if still over: keep the highest-ranked, replace the rest with pointers
other sections are untouched; the output reserve is never borrowed

followUps.question: Where does compaction run?
followUps.html:
Off the critical path where possible, at a threshold.

Trigger:session tokens over the capbackground summariser fills the structured summaryvalidate pinned itemsswap in at the next step

followUps.question: How is this tested?
followUps.html:
At three levels.

Level Test
Unit assembly output for a given state: required items present, under budget
Long-session eval adherence and quality by turn number
Isolation canary data from one tenant never appears for another

followUps.question: What would you build first?
followUps.html:
The assembler with per-section token counts in the trace.

  • It makes every later decision measurable.
  • Then: compaction, then long-term memory, each justified by what the counts and quality curves show.

dontSay: "We store the chat history and send it." — that's no design.
"Memory is a vector database." — say the write, read and eviction rules.
"We'll add limits if it gets expensive." — budgets shape the design.
"It handles long conversations." — show quality by turn number.

mcp-context-engineering-q25.testing: that you measured what was in the window, chose a lever (compaction, state outside the window, isolation, ordering), and can say what you gave up.
mcp-context-engineering-q25.trap: a prompt-wording story dressed up as context engineering.
mcp-context-engineering-q25.spoken:
Beat Say
1 · The decision it served "In my AI interviewer, the model that speaks to the candidate has to answer within a conversational turn, and it has to stay on the interview plan for forty-five minutes."
2 · The constraint "A voice turn has well under a second for everything, so a long prompt wasn't affordable. And an interview is long: if the whole transcript went into every call, each turn would be slower and costlier than the last, and the plan would get buried."
3 · Options weighed "I weighed three options: send the full transcript, summarise it inside the prompt every turn, or keep the state outside the window and inject a slice."
4 · What I built "I chose the third. The speaker sees only the last eight messages. The plan, the moves already delivered and the analysis live in typed state. The decision about what to ask next is code, so it doesn't depend on the model's memory at all. Older turns are meant to be covered by a running summary written by a background task."
5 · What broke "What I gave up is recall of exact wording from early in the interview on the speaking path. <fill: a concrete case where the missing early context mattered, and how you handled it>."
6 · The number "<fill: tokens per turn before → after, or turn latency, or cost per interview>."
Close "The prompt barely changed. What changed was what the model was given."
